script: My boss demanded "100% compliance"—now my crew is literally trapped.. I was on site for Company A, doing a routine run on four inverters. While setting up, I spotted a cracked module left by a rock. I snapped a pic, logged its spot, and kept moving. I called the other tech, asked him to grab a spare module from the container, then finished the inverter job. I closed that ticket, opened a new one for the module swap, fixed it, closed that, and kept going. At the end of the day the VP—our new boss who'd just retired from the old one—pulled me aside. He said, "Why weren't you managing your tickets correctly?" I shrugged, "Everything we did had a ticket." He said, "You took five minutes off the inverter ticket to look at that module and call the other tech. He spent time loading a module into his truck. That time wasn't logged. You should have logged out of the inverter ticket, opened the module ticket, logged that time, then logged back in." I was like, "I am not doing work for another site. It's all one job, same hourly rate." I swallowed my objection and promised to fix the tickets. That's when the malicious compliance kicked in. For the next few weeks, I and the other techs went from 3‑5 tickets a day to almost 20. I stopped at a piece of trash that blew in, opened a new ticket. I answered a question about someone else's job while I was working on another inverter, logged into that other ticket. I fixed a zip tie, created a ticket. I answered a text from my supervisor, created a ticket. Every little thing became its own ticket. The VP loved it. In the monthly crew‑lead meeting he gushed about how accurate our tickets were, how we set a new standard, and how everyone else needed to step up. He wanted the exact level of micromanagement he'd demanded. So yeah, that malicious compliance backfired. It made my life a nightmare, and my coworkers started to resent me. I got stuck in a cycle of paperwork that didn't reflect real work, and the VP kept cheering it on. FML.
